`nomad` stores fitted mobility models for infectious disease modelling. The
usual workflow is:

1. identify a plausible source mobility dataset;
2. inspect the fitted models available for that dataset;
3. prepare a distance matrix and population vector for the prediction setting;
4. predict a mobility matrix;
5. check warnings and sensitivity to alternative models.

```{r setup}
library(nomad)
```

## Available Data And Models

The mobility catalogue describes the datasets used to fit the models in the
package. Looking through it helps us find data collected in settings similar to
our own, taking account of when movement was measured, whose journeys were
recorded and the size of the regions. These details will help us decide which
models are worth exploring for our analysis.

```{r}
mobility_table()
```

Some datasets are included in the catalogue because they may be useful for
future analyses, although we do not yet have their fitted models. The
`has_fitted_models` column lets us identify which datasets already have models
that we can use. We can then look at the model catalogue to see the available
variants and how well each fit the source data. For example, the following
returns all the models fit to data from Zambia.

```{r}
model_table(country = "ZMB")
```

## Inspect A Model

Let's choose the normalised exponential gravity model fit to the newer Zambia
Facebook data. We can use `model_profile()` to see the number of source regions,
their populations and distances, and the period represented by a prediction.
This gives us a starting point for comparing the source setting with our own.

```{r}
model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm
model_profile(model)
```

We can then look at how well the model reproduced the observed trips using
`check()` and `plot()`. These saved summaries are included even when the
underlying trip observations cannot be shared publicly. The
[model selection vignette](selecting-a-model.html) explains how to interpret them.

```{r}
check(model, plots = FALSE)
plot(model)
```

## Prepare A Small Prediction Setting

To predict movement, we need a distance matrix `D` and a population vector `N`
for our regions. These are the same inputs used by `mobility::predict()`. If the
origins and destinations have different populations, they can instead be supplied
as `N_orig` and `N_dest`.

Here we construct a small example with five place names. The populations and
coordinates are invented to show how to arrange the inputs, and should not be
used as estimates for those places. We multiply the distances between the
coordinates by 120 to give our example distances in kilometres. For your own
analysis, you could prepare these inputs from a shapefile and population data,
as shown in the [README example](https://ojwatson.github.io/nomad/).

```{r, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to construct the example regions"}
places <- data.frame(
  name = c("Lusaka", "Kabwe", "Ndola", "Kitwe", "Livingstone"),
  x = c(0, 1.2, 2.8, 2.6, -1.4),
  y = c(0, 1.0, 2.7, 2.4, -2.7),
  population = c(2500000, 230000, 475000, 690000, 170000)
)

D <- as.matrix(dist(places[, c("x", "y")])) * 120
dimnames(D) <- list(places$name, places$name)
N <- setNames(places$population, places$name)
newdata <- list(D = D, N = N)
```

## Make A Prediction

We can now pass the distances and populations to `predict()`, specifying that
our distances are in kilometres. You will see warnings because these five
regions contain a smaller population and cover fewer locations than the data
used to fit the model. The prediction can still be calculated, but those
warnings help us identify differences between our example and the setting in
which the model was fit.

```{r}
M <- predict(model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
round(M / 1000, 1)
```

The result is a matrix in which rows identify the origin of a trip and columns
identify its destination. We have divided the values by 1,000 to make them easier
to read, so a value of 2 represents 2,000 predicted trips. These are counts of
trips, to which a person may contribute more than once. The period is taken from
the model metadata and is 21 days for this fit. The names on the distance matrix and population vector must identify the same regions so that
`nomad` can match each population to the correct location.

For a real analysis, we would now consider whether the model describes movement
at a suitable scale for our question. For example, a model fit to movement between
districts may tell us little about journeys between neighbourhoods within a city.
Comparing alternatives is useful when several models could plausibly describe
the movement we want to study.

## Predict for the source regions

The fitted model also includes the distances and populations used for fitting.
These inputs are often called covariates. We can reuse them to predict movement
for the original regions, which provides a useful comparison with predictions
for a new setting.

```{r}
source_data <- model$get_model()$data[c("D", "N_orig", "N_dest")]
M_source <- predict(model, newdata = source_data)
M_source[1:5, 1:5]
```

## Choose a prediction period

If we want a prediction for a different time period, we can supply `duration`
in days or a `date_start`/`date_end` pair. This scales the prediction in
proportion to the period recorded in the model metadata, assuming that the
average daily trip rate stays constant. For example, the request below uses
30 / 21 as its multiplier because the newer Facebook models predict trip counts
over 21 days. The dates over which data were collected are stored separately
and do not determine this multiplier.

```{r}
M_30 <- predict(model, newdata = source_data, duration = 30)
attr(M_30, "duration_scale")
```

The returned `duration_scale` is the multiplier applied to the original
prediction, in this case approximately 1.43.

Models can also be shared through `nomad` with incomplete source metadata, as
with the earlier Zambia Facebook and CDR models from 2020. Without a prediction
period, we can explore their unscaled predictions but cannot convert the counts
to trips over a specified number of days. The package warns when returning such
a prediction and raises an error if we request a duration conversion. This makes
the available models accessible while showing where missing information limits
their use in an analysis.

## Compare Alternatives

Several models were fit to the Zambia Facebook observations. We can compare
their fit statistics and use `model_weights()` to calculate weights from one of
those measures. Here we use root mean squared error (RMSE), which gives more
weight to models that reproduced the source observations more closely. This
comparison uses models fit to the same dataset, so their errors refer to the
same observed trips.

```{r}
weights <- model_weights(data_name = "zmb_fb_2025", metric = "RMSE")
weights[, c("name", "RMSE", "weight")]
```

We can also use `nomad_ensemble()` to combine predictions from several models.
For a simple example, we will select the exponential departure-diffusion model
and combine it with the gravity model used above. Both were fit to the same
Facebook dataset. Because we ask each model to predict for the same regions and
period, we can take a weighted average of their predicted trip counts. We choose weights of 0.5 for this example, giving each model equal
influence, rather than deriving the weights from their fit statistics.

```{r}
departure_model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp
ensemble <- nomad_ensemble(
  list(departure = departure_model, gravity = model),
  weights = c(departure = 0.5, gravity = 0.5)
)
M_ensemble <- predict(ensemble, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
round(sum(M_ensemble))
```

## Explore parameter uncertainty

So far we have used the mean fitted parameters to make each prediction. Setting
`nsim` to a value greater than one instead gives repeated predictions using
approximate parameter draws from the stored means and standard deviations.
The summary below reports how much the total number of trips and the number
between different regions vary across those draws. This captures parameter
uncertainty within the selected model, while comparing alternative models lets
us explore uncertainty about the choice of model itself.

```{r}
draws <- predict(model, newdata = source_data, nsim = 10, seed = 1)
uncertainty_summary(draws, metrics = c("total", "between_region"))
```

To explore these choices further, [Selecting a mobility model](selecting-a-model.html)
works through the warnings and uncertainty summaries in more detail, and shows
how to compare predictions from several models. Once you have a set of plausible
models, [Identifying a mobility model for an outbreak](outbreak-model-selection.html)
shows how to compare them using the daily incidence of a simulated outbreak.
